passage: Shalini had come home to the village near Madurai after her job interview, sure it was out of her hands now. "If it's in my fate, I'll get it," she said, and stretched out on the thinnai. Her Kavitha chithi was already out in the field, checking the channels before the rain. Shalini watched her all afternoon: pulling weeds, mending a broken bund, talking to the neighbour about seed. At dusk, Chithi lit the lamp before the small shrine and said, as she always did, "Whatever God has written will come." Shalini asked, half teasing, "Then why work so hard?" Chithi laughed. "God writes. I still have to carry the water." That night Shalini opened her laptop and sent the thank-you email she'd been skipping.

qa.q: What did Chithi say when Shalini asked why she worked so hard?
qa.a: "God writes. I still have to carry the water."

qa.q: Why did Shalini feel she could just rest after the interview?
qa.a: Believing the result was already in fate's hands made further effort feel unnecessary, and resting felt like trust rather than avoidance.

qa.q: What choice did Shalini make after watching Chithi?
qa.a: She sent the thank-you email she'd been skipping, doing her own part while still trusting the outcome.

qa.q: How does Kavitha chithi hold faith and effort together?
qa.a: For Chithi, trusting what God has written sits easily beside mending bunds and pulling weeds; the prayer and the work belong to the same day.

grounding: A young adult watches her aunt trust fate and still work hard, and sees that belief need not cancel effort.

passage: Jamal used to think his flatmate Bilal was a contradiction. Before his accountancy exams in Birmingham, Bilal would say, "It's in God's hands, inshallah," and then study at the kitchen table until two in the morning. When the results came, Bilal passed and said, "Alhamdulillah, it was written." Jamal finally asked him about it over tea. "If it's written, why kill yourself studying?" Bilal shrugged. "Trusting God doesn't mean sitting on my hands. I do my part, then I leave the rest." Jamal thought about his own habit of saying "whatever happens, happens" and then not revising. He'd always called it being relaxed. Watching Bilal, it looked more like hiding. The next morning he printed out a study plan of his own.

qa.q: Until what time did Bilal study at the kitchen table?
qa.a: Until two in the morning.

qa.q: Why did Jamal see Bilal as a contradiction at first?
qa.a: Jamal assumed that trusting God with the outcome should make hard study unnecessary, so doing both seemed inconsistent.

qa.q: What turning point led Jamal to print a study plan?
qa.a: Hearing Bilal say he does his part and then leaves the rest, which made Jamal see his own "whatever happens" as hiding rather than calm.

qa.q: How does Bilal see the link between faith and effort?
qa.a: For Bilal they fit together: trust in God covers the outcome, while study is his own responsibility, so he feels no conflict.

grounding: A young man observes his flatmate trusting God and still studying hard, and realises belief need not cancel responsibility.

passage: At the insurance office, Preeti had noticed something about Vijay sir, the senior claims officer. Every morning he touched the small Ganesh idol on his desk and murmured a prayer. When anyone worried about appraisals, he'd say, "Karma will decide." Yet he was the one who stayed back to double-check every file, who taught the juniors the new claims system, who never missed a deadline. One afternoon Preeti asked him, carefully, whether believing in karma didn't make effort pointless. Vijay sir smiled. "Karma is what you do, Preeti. Not what you wait for." She sat with that for a while. She had been telling herself the promotion list was destiny and hadn't updated her training record in months. That evening she stayed back and finished it.

qa.q: What does Vijay sir touch every morning?
qa.a: The small Ganesh idol on his desk.

qa.q: Why had Preeti let her training record slide?
qa.a: Calling the promotion list destiny made her effort feel beside the point, which quietly excused her from updating the record.

qa.q: What choice did Preeti make after the conversation, and why?
qa.a: She stayed back and finished the training record, because Vijay sir's words showed her that faith in karma still asks for action.

qa.q: How does Vijay sir see karma differently from Preeti?
qa.a: For Vijay sir karma is made by what you do, so prayer and hard work go together, while Preeti had treated it as something to wait for.

grounding: A young employee observes a senior colleague who trusts karma yet works diligently, and sees belief need not cancel responsibility.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,
You asked what my father meant when he said "it's all in the stars" at the wedding. I've been thinking about it since. Papa checks the almanac before every big step and says whatever is written will happen. I used to think that meant he left things to fate. Then I watched him this year. When the shop's permit was delayed, he said, "Karma will sort it," and then went to the municipal office four times, with every paper copied twice. When I asked how those fit together, he laughed. "God decides the harvest. I still plough the field." I think I understand now. He trusts something bigger, and it seems to make him calmer, not lazier.
Love,
Reena

qa.q: How many times did Papa go to the municipal office?
qa.a: He went to the municipal office four times.

qa.q: Why did Reena's view of Papa's belief change?
qa.a: Watching him chase the permit with every paper copied twice showed Reena that trusting fate didn't make him passive; if anything it seemed to calm him.

qa.q: What choice did Papa make when the permit was delayed, and what does it show?
qa.a: He said karma would sort it and still went to the office four times with copies; trust in larger forces and doing his own part went together.

qa.q: How might Yusuf understand Papa's words after reading the letter?
qa.a: Yusuf might see 'it's all in the stars' not as giving up but as a way to stay calm while still working hard.

grounding: A young person notices that their father trusts fate and karma while still working hard, and sees the two need not clash.

passage: Madhav, you laughed when my Ajji said the new tiffin contract was "up to Chamundeshwari". I laughed too, once. But I stayed with her in Mysuru for three weeks this summer, and I watched. Every morning she lit the lamp and said, "Whatever is meant will come." Then she was at the stove by five, tasting every dal, checking every box before the delivery boy left. When the college canteen tender came up, she prayed, and she also made me type her menu three times until the prices were exactly right. She got it. When I asked whether it was the goddess or the menu, she tapped my head. "Why do you think it has to be one?" I'm Darshan, and I'm starting to think her faith just meant she didn't panic while she worked.

qa.q: What did Ajji make Darshan do with her menu?
qa.a: She made Darshan type her menu three times until the prices were exactly right.

qa.q: What does Ajji's tap on the head suggest she thinks of Darshan's question?
qa.a: She seems amused and sure; for her, trusting the goddess and doing the work belong together, so choosing one seems a silly split.

qa.q: What in Ajji's approach could Darshan use in daily work?
qa.a: Keeping a belief that brings calm while still doing the careful parts, like checking every box, so faith steadies the effort instead of replacing it.

qa.q: How might Madhav see Ajji differently after hearing this?
qa.a: Madhav might stop seeing her words as passive and notice discipline and trust working side by side.

grounding: A young adult watches a grandmother trust in the goddess while working carefully and sees that faith and effort can coexist.

passage: Arnab sits at the desk next to mine in the government office in Kolkata. Every morning he touches the small photo of his family deity before switching on his computer. When the promotion list was announced, he said calmly, "What is written will happen." I assumed that meant he wouldn't prepare for the departmental exam. I was wrong. He stayed late every evening for six weeks, working through old papers. When I asked, half teasing, why he bothered if fate would decide, he smiled. "Fate decides the result. I decide the effort. Both are my dharma." I didn't know what to say. I'd always thought believing in destiny meant sitting back. When the results came, he passed. He touched the photo again, same as always. I'm Tanuja, and I've started thinking about my own beliefs differently.

qa.q: What does Arnab touch every morning before switching on his computer?
qa.a: A small photo of his family deity.

qa.q: How did Tanuja feel when Arnab explained his view of fate and effort?
qa.a: Tanuja felt surprised and thoughtful, unsure what to say, since Tanuja had assumed believing in destiny meant sitting back.

qa.q: What can someone learn from Arnab's approach?
qa.a: You can hold a belief in fate and still work hard, doing your full part and leaving the rest to larger forces.

qa.q: How does Arnab seem to see fate and effort?
qa.a: Arnab seems calm and at peace, seeing fate and effort as working together, both part of his duty.

grounding: It shows a colleague noticing a man who trusts destiny and still works hard, learning that belief in fate need not cancel personal responsibility.

passage:
A Monday in March. Jyoti watched her husband Nitin light the lamp before the deity at dawn. "Whatever Bhagwan has written for the exam, will happen," he murmured. Jyoti felt a flicker of worry. Would he stop studying?

The Thursday after. At midnight, she found him still at the dining table, surrounded by the civil services notes, eyes red. "You said it's written," she whispered, half joking. Nitin smiled. "It's written that I'll try with everything. The result is His. The effort is mine."

A Saturday in June. The results came. Nitin hadn't cleared the final list. He lit the lamp the same way, then sat with the notebook. "Again next year," he said. Jyoti had expected despair. Instead there was calm. She sat beside him, feeling a strange steadiness herself, and began to organise his papers for another year.

qa.q: What did Nitin do at dawn?
qa.a: He lit the lamp before the deity.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel when she first heard Nitin say the exam result was written?
qa.a: She felt a flicker of worry that his belief in fate might stop him studying.

qa.q: What can Jyoti learn from Nitin's response to the result?
qa.a: That trust in a larger plan can bring calm after disappointment while still leading to fresh effort, like planning again for next year.

qa.q: How does Nitin seem to experience his faith and his effort?
qa.a: Nitin seems steady and at peace, seeing the effort as his and the result as God's, so failure doesn't crush him.

grounding: It shows a wife observing her husband combine trust in destiny with hard work, noticing that belief in larger forces need not cancel personal responsibility, over several months.

passage: Saurabh, you ask whether believing in karma makes a person lazy. Let me tell you about my father-in-law, the year I married into his family. I was a young bride of twenty-four in a village near Varanasi. Babuji believed everything was in God's hands. Every morning he said, "Karma is what I do; the fruit is His." I thought that meant he would just wait for rain. But that year the rains were late. Babuji was out at four every morning, digging channels from the pond to the fields, carrying water in buckets with the other farmers. When the crop came, it was small, but it came. He bowed at the temple and said, "Bhagwan gave what He gave." I learned from Babuji that faith and effort sit together. That's what Himani wants you to remember, beta.

qa.q: What did Babuji dig every morning when the rains were late?
qa.a: Channels from the pond to the fields.

qa.q: How did young Himani feel watching Babuji's belief in fate at first?
qa.a: Himani felt doubtful, thinking his faith meant he would just wait, and was surprised to see him working so hard.

qa.q: What turning point in the story showed how faith and effort fit together?
qa.a: When the rains were late and Babuji still dug channels and carried water, it showed that trusting God did not stop him from doing his part.

qa.q: How might Babuji have felt when the small crop came?
qa.a: Babuji likely felt grateful and accepting, bowing at the temple, content that he had done his part.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how she observed her father-in-law trust destiny and still work hard, learning that belief in larger forces need not cancel responsibility.

passage:
The power had gone again in Lucknow, and the shop's fans stood still. Yusuf, twenty-four, sat at the counter of his father's electrical-parts shop while Abbu counted the day's slips by torchlight.
Yusuf had always thought his father left everything to fate. Abbu said “Allah's will” about every good or bad month.
But tonight Yusuf watched closely. Abbu checked every slip twice. He called three late-paying customers, politely. He wrote tomorrow's orders in his neat notebook.
Yusuf's friend Santosh came by with sweets for his sister's engagement. “Your father works like a machine, yaar.”
“He says it's all destiny,” Yusuf said.
Abbu looked up. “Destiny is Allah's. The notebook is mine.”
Yusuf laughed. For the first time, he saw that his father trusted something larger and still worked as if every slip mattered.

qa.q: What did Abbu write in his neat notebook?
qa.a: He wrote tomorrow's orders.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel as he watched his father tonight?
qa.a: Yusuf felt surprised and newly understanding, seeing that trust in destiny and hard work sat together in his father.

qa.q: What could Yusuf take from his father's example?
qa.a: That he can hold his own faith or sense of destiny and still take full responsibility for his work.

qa.q: How might Abbu see his own faith and work?
qa.a: Abbu seems calm and clear: destiny belongs to God, but the careful work is his own responsibility.

grounding: The passage shows a young man noticing that his father trusts destiny and still works hard, so belief in larger forces need not cancel responsibility.

passage:
Chandrika worked beside Dilnaz Aunty at a garment export unit in Tiruppur. Dilnaz Aunty was sixty and had worked there for thirty years.
Every morning Dilnaz Aunty touched her forehead and said, “What is written will happen.” At first Chandrika, twenty-five, thought that meant she didn't bother about anything.
But week by week Chandrika noticed. Dilnaz Aunty checked every seam twice. She taught new girls the quicker cutting method. When her son was ill, she arranged the shift swap herself and came back to finish her quota.
One lunchtime, Chandrika asked, “Aunty, if it's all written, why work so hard?”
Dilnaz Aunty laughed. “Maybe what is written is that I work hard.”
Chandrika smiled. She had been using “fate” as a reason to stop trying on her own supervisor exam. That evening she opened her books again.

qa.q: What did Chandrika decide to do, and why is it wise?

“Yes, Abhinav. Third time.”
“Your Biji always says it's all in Waheguru's hands. Why not just wait?”
“That's the funny thing. I used to think that too. That if it's written, why try?”

Abhinav laughed. “So God gets the result, and you get the homework.”

passage:
I'm Kunal, and my flatmate Divyansh confused me for a long time.
Every morning he lit a small diya in front of a picture of Ganesha and said, "Whatever is written will happen." I grew up hearing that line from my grandmother too, and I'd always taken it to mean: so why try?
But Divyansh was preparing for the civil services, and he tried harder than anyone I knew. Up at five, newspaper notes, mock tests every Sunday. When I asked how that fitted with "whatever is written," he shrugged. "I do my karma. The result isn't mine to hold. That's what lets me sleep."
I watched him after a bad mock test. He was disappointed, but he didn't collapse. He prayed, and then he took out the answer key and marked every mistake.
I realised I'd been using fate as an excuse. He was using it as a kind of peace.

qa.q: What did Divyansh do every Sunday?
qa.a: He took mock tests every Sunday.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel watching Divyansh after the bad mock test?
qa.a: Kunal felt surprised and a little humbled, realising that fate had been an excuse for Kunal while for Divyansh it was a source of peace.

qa.q: What could Kunal take from Divyansh's approach?
qa.a: Kunal could hold on to faith in a larger plan while still doing daily work, like Divyansh marking every mistake after a bad test.

qa.q: How does Divyansh seem to see the link between fate and effort?
qa.a: Divyansh sees doing his karma as his job and the result as not his to hold, which lets him work hard and still sleep calmly.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing that a friend trusts destiny and still works hard, so belief in larger forces need not cancel personal responsibility.

Supervisor's note, site engineering team — Francis
Vaibhav joined us in March. Each morning before the site meeting he touches the small Hanuman picture on his helmet and says, "Upar wale ki marzi." In the first week I assumed he left things to fate.
I was wrong. He double-checks every measurement. When the slab pour was delayed by rain, he said, "That is in God's hands," and then spent two hours redoing the schedule, which was in his.
I grew up in a home where people said the same things, and I used to think faith meant waiting. Watching Vaibhav, I see it differently. He seems calmer about what he can't control, and more careful about what he can.
I asked him about it last week. He said, "Bhagwan decides the weather. I decide if the formwork is ready."
I have asked him to mentor the two new trainees.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav do when the slab pour was delayed by rain?
qa.a: He said, "That is in God's hands," and then spent two hours redoing the schedule.

qa.q: What did the supervisor feel on realising the first impression of Vaibhav was wrong?
qa.a: The supervisor felt surprised and thoughtful, seeing that faith did not mean waiting, but could sit alongside careful work.

qa.q: Why is Vaibhav a good choice to mentor the new trainees?
qa.a: He shows how to accept what is outside one's control, like weather, while taking full responsibility for what is, like measurements and schedules.

qa.q: How might the trainees see Vaibhav's morning ritual?
qa.a: The trainees might see it at first as simple habit, then notice that it goes together with the most careful checking on the site.

grounding: It shows, through a supervisor's note, someone noticing that a colleague trusts destiny and still takes responsibility, so larger beliefs need not cancel personal effort.

passage:
Tuesday night
Chandrika aunty, who runs the flower stall outside the temple, said something today I keep thinking about. I'm Uday, and I've been helping her on weekends since I lost my job.
I asked her how she stays so calm when sales are bad. She said, "Kismat decides some days. Rain, a festival moved, a new stall opening. I can't touch that."
Then she told me how she picks marigolds at four in the morning, keeps a notebook of which days sell best, and moved her stall two metres to catch the bus queue. "That part is mine," she said. "Bhagwan gives the day. I give the work."
I've been saying "it's all destiny" for three months and doing nothing. She says it and does everything.
Tomorrow I'm updating my CV. Destiny can handle the rest.

qa.q: Why did Chandrika aunty move her stall two metres?
qa.a: She moved it to catch the bus queue.

qa.q: How does Uday feel after talking with Chandrika aunty?
qa.a: Uday feels a bit ashamed of three months of doing nothing, but also newly motivated to act.

qa.q: What will Uday do next, and why does it follow from her example?
qa.a: Uday will update the CV tomorrow, copying her way of leaving the uncontrollable to destiny while doing the controllable work.

qa.q: How does Chandrika aunty seem to see her own success?
qa.a: She sees it as partly kismat and partly her own work, like early picking and careful notes, and she stays calm about the rest.

grounding: It shows a young adult noticing that a stall owner trusts destiny and still works hard, realising that belief in larger forces need not cancel personal responsibility.
